newsitem.title: GERMANY: ATHLETICS-KRABBE LOSES APPEAL AGAINST DOPING BAN.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-KRABBE LOSES APPEAL AGAINST DOPING BAN.

text.p: Former double world sprint champion Katrin Krabbe's hopes of winning compensation for a much-publicised doping ban suffered another setback on Thursday when she lost an appeal in the German civil courts.
A federal court upheld a ruling that the German athletics federation (DLV) was within its rights to ban Krabbe after she admitted to taking the banned drug clenbuterol in 1992.
Krabbe, who has since given up athletics, married a lawyer and started a family, now looks very unlikely to get any money at all from athletics authorities despite five years of legal battles.
"The case is buried. I am very relieved," DLV general secretary Jan Kern said after the ruling which has saved the German federation from possible financial problems.
In a decision published on Thursday, the Federal Court of Justice in Karlsruhe rejected an appeal by Krabbe against a Munich court's verdict last year in favour of the DLV.

The latest decision does not affect the 1991 double world champion's right to sue the International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) over a separate suspension in 1993 which proved to be illegal under German law.
But Krabbe is not expected to win huge compensation from the international federation since most of her sponsorship contracts had been terminated before the IAAF ban.
Indeed the IAAF seems so confident of not having to pay out that it has already dropped an appeal against the court ruling.

DLV lawyer Clemens Prokop said Krabbe would now have to pay costs of up to 50,000 marks ($28,300), adding that the ruling meant it was very unlikely that Krabbe would win the one million marks ($567,000) she wants from the IAAF.

Krabbe admitted taking clenbuterol in 1992 after a positive test. But the DLV and IAAF were unable to impose the mandatory four-year ban because of a legal problem with the German federation's rulebook.
Instead the DLV, which has since solved the problem in its rules, imposed a one-year ban for unsportsmanlike conduct in 1992.
The IAAF added a further two-year suspension in 1993. The Munich court ruled last year that the DLV had acted within the law while the IAAF had acted illegally.
The Federal Court of Justice agreed that the DLV should not have to pay any damages. ($ = 1.763 German Marks)
